title: Advanced LVM: snapshots
objective: Create, use and merge LVM snapshots to capture and roll back a logical volume.

questions.q: What is an LVM snapshot?
options: A point-in-time copy of a logical volume that only stores changed blocks
A full independent copy of the volume
A backup stored off the disk
A read-only clone that never changes
questions.explain: Snapshots use copy-on-write, so they start tiny and grow as the origin changes.

questions.q: What happens if a snapshot's allocated space fills up completely?
options: The snapshot becomes invalid (dropped) and can no longer be used
questions.explain: Size the snapshot for the expected amount of change, or enable auto-extend in lvm.conf.

questions.q: Which command reverts an origin volume to its snapshot's state?
questions.explain: If the origin is in use, the merge happens at the next activation/reboot.

questions.q: In `lvs`, which columns tell you a snapshot's origin and how full it is?
questions.explain: Watch Data% — at 100% the snapshot is lost.

questions.q: Why take a snapshot before a risky upgrade or edit?
options: You can quickly roll the volume back to the pre-change state if it breaks
questions.explain: Snapshots are a fast local "undo" — not a replacement for real backups.

questions.q: A snapshot is best used as a stable source for:
options: Taking a consistent backup while the origin keeps changing
questions.explain: Back up from the frozen snapshot, then remove it.

questions.q: Create a 1 GiB snapshot named datasnap of the logical volume /dev/vgdata/lvdata.
questions.explain: -s makes it a snapshot; the origin is the last argument.

questions.q: Show all logical volumes including snapshots, with their origin and usage.
questions.explain: `lvs -a` reveals hidden internal volumes; add columns to see snapshot detail.

questions.q: Merge the snapshot /dev/vgdata/datasnap back into its origin.
questions.explain: After merging, the snapshot is automatically removed.

labs.title: Snapshot, break, and roll back (exam-plus)
labs.scenario: On lvdata (mounted at /mnt/data with a file inside), take a snapshot, deliberately corrupt the data, then roll back using the snapshot and prove the file returned.
verify: cat /mnt/data/report.txt      # shows "good version"

labs.title: Consistent backup from a snapshot
labs.scenario: Snapshot lvdata, mount the snapshot read-only, back it up with tar, then remove the snapshot.
verify: tar -tzf /root/data-backup.tar.gz | head; lvs | grep -c bsnap   # 0 left

labs.title: Watch a snapshot fill up
labs.scenario: Create a small (100 MiB) snapshot, then write more than 100 MiB into the origin and observe the snapshot become invalid.
steps: lvs -a -o +data_percent      # tiny shows 100% then goes invalid
verify: lvs shows the snapshot invalidated (Attr has an 'I'); you understand sizing

title: Advanced LVM: thin, striped and RAID volumes
objective: Build thin-provisioned, striped and mirrored/RAID logical volumes.

questions.q: What is thin provisioning in LVM?
options: Logical volumes can present more space than is physically allocated, using a shared thin pool
Volumes that are always exactly their physical size
questions.explain: Space is consumed from the pool only as data is written.

questions.q: What is the main risk of thin provisioning?
options: Over-provisioning: if the pool fills, writes to any thin volume fail
questions.explain: Monitor the pool's Data% and Meta% and extend before it fills.

questions.q: A striped logical volume (`--type striped -i 2`) improves:
options: Performance, by spreading I/O across multiple physical volumes
questions.explain: Striping has no redundancy; losing one PV loses the volume.

questions.q: Which LVM RAID type gives mirroring (redundancy) across two devices?
questions.explain: raid1 keeps a full copy on each leg; it survives one device failing.

questions.q: In `lvcreate --type raid5 -i 3`, what does -i specify?
options: The number of data stripes (RAID 5 also adds one parity's worth of space)
questions.explain: RAID 5 needs at least 3 devices and tolerates one failure.

questions.q: Which command shows the underlying devices and segment type of LVs?
questions.explain: It reveals which PVs each stripe/leg sits on.

questions.q: Create a 1 GiB thin pool named tpool in volume group vgdata.
questions.explain: -T (or --type thin-pool) builds the pool that thin volumes draw from.

questions.q: Create a 5 GiB thin volume named tvol from the thin pool vgdata/tpool.
questions.explain: -V is the virtual size, which may exceed the pool's real size.

questions.q: Create a striped LV named fast across 2 PVs, 1 GiB total, 64 KiB stripe size.
questions.explain: -i = number of stripes (PVs), -I = stripe size in KiB.

questions.q: Create a mirrored (raid1) LV named safe of 500 MiB in vgdata.
questions.explain: -m 1 means one mirror copy (two legs total).

labs.title: Thin provisioning end to end
labs.scenario: In vgdata create a 1 GiB thin pool, a 4 GiB thin volume, format and mount it, and watch pool usage grow as you write.
steps: lvs vgdata      # tpool Data% climbs toward 300 MiB used
verify: df -h /mnt/thin shows 4G; lvs shows the pool is only partly used

labs.title: Build and inspect a RAID1 volume
labs.scenario: Create a raid1 LV across two PVs, format and mount it, then show its legs and sync status.
verify: lvs -a shows two rimage/rmeta legs and 100% sync

labs.title: Extend a thin pool before it fills
labs.scenario: Simulate a nearly full thin pool and extend the pool (not just the volume) to avoid write failures.
steps: lvs vgdata      # Data% drops as capacity grows
verify: the pool has more free space and thin volumes keep working

labs.title: Compare striped vs linear (concept + build)
labs.scenario: Create one linear and one striped LV of the same size and explain when you would choose each.
verify: # linear = simple/flexible; striped = faster I/O, no redundancy

title: Advanced storage: Stratis, VDO and recovery
objective: Use Stratis pools, LVM-VDO dedup/compression, and recover LVM metadata.

questions.q: What is Stratis?
options: A local storage-management layer that builds pools and thin XFS filesystems on top of LVM/device-mapper
questions.explain: You manage it with the `stratis` command and the stratisd service.

questions.q: How do you make a Stratis filesystem mount at boot in /etc/fstab?
questions.explain: The device is not ready until stratisd runs, so the mount must wait for it.

questions.q: What does LVM-VDO provide?
options: Inline deduplication and compression, so a volume stores more logical data than physical space
questions.explain: VDO is ideal for backups/VM images with lots of repeated data.

questions.q: Where does LVM keep automatic backups of volume-group metadata?
questions.explain: These let you restore a VG's metadata after accidental damage.

questions.q: Which command restores a volume group's metadata from an LVM backup file?
questions.explain: Pair it with vgcfgbackup, which writes the current metadata to a file.

questions.q: To physically move a volume group's disks to another system, you first:
options: Deactivate its LVs and run vgexport, then vgimport on the new host
questions.explain: vgexport marks the VG as movable; vgimport reactivates it elsewhere.

questions.q: Create a Stratis pool named mypool from the disk /dev/vdb.
questions.explain: Install stratisd/stratis-cli and enable stratisd first.

questions.q: Create a Stratis filesystem named data in the pool mypool.
questions.explain: It appears at /dev/stratis/mypool/data.

questions.q: Back up the current metadata of volume group vgdata to a file.
questions.explain: By default it writes to /etc/lvm/backup/vgdata.

labs.title: Stratis pool and filesystem at boot
labs.scenario: Install Stratis, build a pool on a spare disk, create a filesystem, and mount it persistently at /mnt/stratis.
verify: stratis filesystem list; findmnt /mnt/stratis; reboot and re-check

labs.title: Grow a Stratis pool
labs.scenario: Add a second disk to your Stratis pool and confirm the extra capacity appears.
verify: the pool's total size increased with no downtime

labs.title: Deduplication with LVM-VDO
labs.scenario: Create a VDO volume, format and mount it, write duplicate data, and show that physical usage stays low.
steps: for i in $(seq 1 5); do cp /root/bigfile /mnt/vdo/copy$i; done
verify: logical data far exceeds the physical space actually used

labs.title: Recover a damaged volume group
labs.scenario: Back up vgdata's metadata, "accidentally" remove an LV, then restore the metadata from the archive.
steps: lvs vgdata      # note an LV to sacrifice, e.g. lvtest
ls /etc/lvm/archive/ | grep vgdata      # find the pre-removal archive
verify: lvs vgdata shows lvtest restored (reactivate with vgchange -ay vgdata)

title: Advanced SELinux: troubleshooting denials
objective: Read AVC denials and generate custom policy with audit2allow.

questions.q: Where are SELinux AVC (access-vector-cache) denials logged?
questions.explain: Search them with ausearch; if auditd is off they may appear in the journal/messages.

questions.q: Which command searches the audit log for recent AVC denials?
questions.explain: -m AVC filters the message type; -ts recent limits the time window.

questions.q: What does audit2why do?
options: Explains WHY an SELinux denial happened (often suggesting a boolean or context fix)
questions.explain: It reads denials and gives human-readable reasons.

questions.q: What does `audit2allow -a -M mymod` produce?
options: A loadable policy module (mymod.pp) that allows the denied actions
questions.explain: You then load it with `semodule -i mymod.pp`.

questions.q: Before writing a custom module for a denial, you should first check whether:
options: A boolean or a correct file/port label already fixes it (the preferred solution)
The service should run as root
questions.explain: Custom modules are a last resort; labels and booleans fix most issues.

questions.q: The setroubleshoot tool `sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log` gives you:
options: Plain-language analysis of denials with suggested fixes
questions.explain: Install setroubleshoot-server to get sealert and desktop alerts.

questions.q: Putting one domain into "permissive" (e.g. httpd_t) while keeping the rest enforcing is done with:
questions.explain: This logs (but allows) only that domain's denials — great for targeted troubleshooting.

questions.q: Show recent SELinux denials from the audit log.
questions.explain: Add `| audit2why` to see the reason for each denial.

questions.q: Generate and name a policy module "myweb" from all current denials.
questions.explain: Review the generated myweb.te before loading myweb.pp.

questions.q: Load a compiled SELinux policy module named myweb.pp.
questions.explain: List loaded modules with `semodule -l`; remove with `semodule -r myweb`.

labs.title: Diagnose and fix a real denial (label first)
labs.scenario: Serve a file that has the wrong context so httpd is denied, find the denial, understand it, and fix it the RIGHT way (relabel, not a custom module).
verify: curl http://localhost/ now returns the content

labs.title: Custom module as a last resort
labs.scenario: Create a denial that no boolean fixes (e.g. a service writing to an unusual path), capture it, and build+load a custom module — after confirming no label/boolean solves it.
steps: ausearch -m AVC -ts recent | audit2allow -m custom      # review .te first
verify: the action is now allowed and semodule -l shows "custom"

labs.title: Targeted permissive domain
labs.scenario: Put httpd_t into permissive mode to collect all its denials for a misbehaving app without weakening the rest of the system, then remove it afterward.
steps: # reproduce the app behavior, collect denials with ausearch
verify: only httpd_t was permissive; the rest stayed enforcing

labs.title: Use sealert for a guided fix
labs.scenario: Install setroubleshoot, reproduce a denial, and use sealert to get a step-by-step suggested fix.
verify: you can read the suggested commands and apply the correct one

title: Advanced SELinux: contexts, ports, booleans and confined users
objective: Manage custom file contexts, port labels, booleans and SELinux user mappings.

questions.q: What is the difference between chcon and semanage fcontext + restorecon?
options: chcon changes the label now but is lost on relabel; semanage records it permanently, restorecon applies it
questions.explain: For anything that must survive a relabel, always use semanage fcontext.

questions.q: A file-context rule like `'/web(/.*)?'` uses:
options: A regular expression so the type applies to the directory and everything under it
questions.explain: The `(/.*)?` suffix covers the directory itself and all contents.

questions.q: To let a service listen on a non-standard port under SELinux, you:
options: Add the port to the correct type, e.g. semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888
questions.explain: If the port is already labeled another type, use -m to modify it.

questions.q: What does `semanage boolean -l -C` show?
options: Only the booleans you have changed from their default
questions.explain: Handy for reviewing your customizations.

questions.q: SELinux confined users (user_u, staff_u, sysadm_u) control:
options: What a Linux login is allowed to do at the SELinux level, beyond normal permissions
questions.explain: semanage login maps a Linux user to an SELinux user.

questions.q: Which command maps the Linux user "operator" to the SELinux user staff_u?
questions.explain: See current mappings with `semanage login -l`.

questions.q: After adding many fcontext rules, which single command applies default labels to a whole tree?
questions.explain: restorecon reads the fcontext database and sets each file to its defined type.

questions.q: Add a permanent rule so /web and everything under it is labeled httpd_sys_content_t.
questions.explain: Then apply it with `restorecon -Rv /web`.

questions.q: Let SELinux allow a service to listen on TCP port 8888 as an http port.
questions.explain: Check with `semanage port -l | grep 8888`.

questions.q: List every SELinux boolean related to httpd with its current value.
questions.explain: Toggle persistently with `setsebool -P <boolean> on`.

labs.title: Custom web root on a custom port (full stack)
labs.scenario: Serve /web/index.html on port 8888 in enforcing mode: fix the file context, the port label, and the firewall.
verify: curl http://localhost:8888/ returns "custom"

labs.title: Confine a user with SELinux
labs.scenario: Create a user "guestx", map them to the restrictive user_u SELinux user, and show that the mapping applies.
verify: su - guestx -c 'id -Z' shows user_u:...  (a confined context)

labs.title: Review and reset your SELinux customizations
labs.scenario: List all the fcontext rules, port labels and booleans you have changed, then remove one custom fcontext rule and relabel.
verify: semanage fcontext -l -C no longer lists the /web rule

labs.title: Boolean-driven feature
labs.scenario: Enable httpd to connect to the network and to read user home directories, persistently, and verify.
verify: both booleans report "on" and survive a reboot

title: Advanced SELinux: services, containers and relabeling
objective: Apply SELinux to real services and containers, and relabel a filesystem.

questions.q: Why does moving a file with `mv` often break a service under SELinux?
options: mv preserves the file's original context instead of the destination's default
questions.explain: cp (without -a) or restorecon gives the file the destination's correct type.

questions.q: What does `restorecon -Rv /path` do that chcon does not?
options: It sets each file to the type defined by the fcontext policy (surviving relabels)
questions.explain: restorecon is policy-driven; chcon is a manual, non-persistent override.

questions.q: How do you trigger a full filesystem relabel on the next boot?
questions.explain: The system relabels everything and removes the flag; it can take a while.

questions.q: In `podman run -v /data:/data:Z`, what does the :Z do?
options: Relabels the volume with a private container context so the container can access it
questions.explain: Lowercase :z labels it as shared among containers; :Z is private to one.

questions.q: Rootless containers rely on SELinux type ______ to confine container processes.
questions.explain: SELinux adds a strong isolation layer on top of namespaces.

questions.q: Which tool checks whether a path currently matches its policy-defined context?
questions.explain: It shows the expected label so you can spot mismatches.

questions.q: Dry-run a relabel of /var/www to see what restorecon WOULD change, without changing anything.
questions.explain: -n means "no change"; drop it to actually apply the labels.

questions.q: Show the policy-defined (default) context for the path /web/index.html.
questions.explain: Compare it to the actual label from `ls -Z` to find mismatches.

questions.q: Run a container mounting /srv/data with a private SELinux relabel.
questions.explain: :Z relabels the host directory to container_file_t for that container.

labs.title: Move vs copy and fix the label
labs.scenario: Show how mv breaks a web file's context while cp/restorecon fixes it.
verify: both files now have httpd_sys_content_t

labs.title: Persistent SELinux for a container volume
labs.scenario: Run a rootless container that serves content from a host directory, using the correct SELinux volume label, and make the host label permanent.
steps: podman run -d --name web -p 8080:80 -v /srv/webdata:/usr/share/nginx/html:Z nginx 2>/dev/null || echo "(pull nginx first)"
verify: ls -Z /srv/webdata shows container_file_t; curl localhost:8080 works

labs.title: Full filesystem relabel
labs.scenario: Schedule and perform a full relabel (as you would after fixing widespread context damage), then confirm it ran.
steps: # system relabels during boot, then removes /.autorelabel
verify: getenforce is Enforcing and contexts are correct

labs.title: Audit a directory's contexts
labs.scenario: For /var/www, dry-run restorecon to list any files whose label does not match policy, then fix only those.
steps: restorecon -Rnv /var/www          # lists mismatches without changing them
verify: a second dry run (restorecon -Rnv /var/www) reports nothing to change
